title: Binary String With Substrings Representing 1 To N
statement: You are given a string `s` made only of the characters `'0'` and `'1'`, and a positive integer `n`. For each integer `x` with `1 <= x <= n`, write `x` in binary without leading zeros. Return `true` when every one of these `n` binary forms occurs somewhere in `s` as a contiguous block of characters (a substring), and `false` when at least one of them does not.
notes:
## Intuition

Checking each number from `1` to `n` with a substring search is fine for small `n` but `n` can be `10^9`. Turn it around: enumerate what `s` can offer. A substring that starts with `1` is exactly the binary form of some number, and only substrings worth at most `n` matter. Since a value at least doubles with each extra digit, every start position yields at most about 30 useful substrings. Collect their values in a set; the answer is `true` exactly when the set holds all `n` numbers. This also settles huge `n` quickly, because `s` has too few substrings to cover them.

## Approach

1. Keep a set `seen` of the values found.
2. For each `start`, skip it if `s[start]` is `'0'`: a leading zero never begins a binary form.
3. Extend `end` to the right, building `value` by doubling and adding the new digit.
4. Stop extending once `value > n`; otherwise add `value` to `seen`.
5. Every value in `seen` lies in `[1, n]`, so return `seen.size === n`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "0110"`, `n = 3`. `start = 0` is a `'0'`, so skip it. `start = 1`: `value` becomes `1`, then `3` (`"11"`), then `6` (`"110"`), which is over `3`, so stop; `seen = {1, 3}`. `start = 2`: `1`, then `2` (`"10"`); `seen = {1, 2, 3}`. `start = 3` is a `'0'`. The set has `3` values, equal to `n`, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(|s| · log n): each start extends at most about log₂ n + 1 steps.
- Space: O(min(n, |s| · log n)) for the set.

## Pitfalls

- Looping `x` from `1` to `n` times out when `n` is near `10^9`.
- Substrings with leading zeros must not be counted as separate forms; skipping starts at `'0'` handles this.
- Without the `value > n` break, values grow past 2^53 on a long run of digits and lose precision.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seen` | distinct values in `[1, n]` found as substrings |
| `start` | first index of the current substring |
| `end` | last index of the current substring |
| `value` | the number spelled by `s[start..end]` |

narration.2: The set gathers every number from 1 to n that appears in s.
narration.4: Try each position of s as the first digit of a binary form.
narration.5: A binary form never starts with 0...
narration.6: ...so skip this start; the same numbers are found from a later 1.
narration.8: value will hold the number spelled by s[start..end].
narration.9: Extend the substring one digit to the right.
narration.10: Shift the value left by one bit and add the new digit.
narration.11: Once the value exceeds n, longer substrings only grow larger...
narration.14: This value is between 1 and n, so record it.
narration.17: All recorded values lie in [1, n], so every number is present exactly when there are n of them.
